title: Throughput-Price Elasticity — lab runbook
content:
TL;DR:
Short experiment plan and interim results for the throughput vs price elasticity probe. Goal: quantify incremental $/k-token savings available from (a) increasing slot concurrency, (b) switching instance class, (c) activating 4-bit quant profile, while holding p99 latency budget soft SLOs. This doc is a runbook (lab notes + ASCII charts) intended for product and infra engineers to iterate on parameter space.

Objective:
- Provide a simple, reproducible map: throughput (queries/sec or tokens/sec) vs effective cost-per-1k-tokens under representative session mixes.
- Surface operational regimes where cost savings are large with acceptable latency tradeoffs (p50/p90/p99).
- Capture sensitivity to quantization and instance family.

Testbed and config:
- Model: open-llama-sim-13B (served with Redwood runtime shimbed config for parity).
- Dataset: 10k synthetic chat sessions, session length distribution: 60% short (<=64 tokens), 30% medium (65–512), 10% long (>512).
- Traffic patterns: sustained steady load and microburst pattern (4x baseline for 30s every 5m).
- Instance families: g5x2 (baseline), g5x8 (tall), c7gx4 (dense), and a small on-prem GPU profile (np-rt-1). Note: naming sanitized for doc.
- Concurrency knobs: slot-based (1, 2, 4, 8) and multiplex (dynamic multiplex factor 1–6).
- Quantization profiles: fp16 (baseline), int8, 4bit-qlora-ish (lossy but throughput-friendly).
- Metrics collected: tokens/sec (aggregate), QPS (requests/sec), p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), GPU util (%), energy estimate (W), effective cost ($/1k tokens) computed from instance list price + amortized overhead.

Scenarios (matrix):
- S1 steady, g5x2, slots=1, fp16
- S2 steady, g5x2, slots=4, fp16
- S3 steady, g5x8, slots=2, int8
- S4 microburst, g5x8, multiplex=4, int8
- S5 steady, c7gx4, slots=2, 4bit
- S6 on-prem np-rt-1, steady, slots=4, 4bit (cost modeled)

Representative ASCII result table (aggregated across runs) — canonical row format: scenario | tokens/sec | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | $/1k toks | notes
S1 | 4200 | 65 | 120 | 290 | 0.078 | baseline single-slot fp16, gpu-util 54%
S2 | 8200 | 78 | 160 | 410 | 0.055 | 4 slots increases throughput, p99 worsens ~40%
S3 | 13500 | 95 | 210 | 520 | 0.043 | taller instance amortizes kernel overhead; int8 safe for short/medium sessions
S4 | burst->peak 4x: mean tokens/sec 52000 | p50 110 | p90 240 | p99 890 | burst $/1k toks 0.061 | microburst p99 penalty significant under multiplex
S5 | 17800 | 130 | 280 | 640 | 0.032 | 4bit gives biggest $ savings but higher long-session p99
S6 | 16200 | 90 | 205 | 450 | 0.027 (modeled) | on-prem cheaper per hour but network egress and ops overhead included

Observations / patterns:
- Elasticity sweet spot: moving from single-slot to 2–4 slots yields large tokens/sec uplift for modest p99 inflation; above 4 slots diminishing returns.
- Tall vs narrow: tall instances (g5x8-like) often win on $/1k when session mix includes longer sessions because KV cache and memory locality reduce per-token kernel dispatch overhead.
- Quantization: 4-bit profiles produce the biggest per-token savings but increase variance for long sessions (p99 spike). For conversational workloads with many short turns, 4-bit is a clear win in modeled cost.
- Microburst fragility: multiplexing helps throughput during steady periods but microbursts produce outsized p99 latency; we saw p99 ~2x relative to steady on same instance when multiplex is high.
- On-prem model: competitive on $/1k when utilization >60% sustained and ops overhead is kept low.

Sensitivity notes (quick):
- If model size grows +20% tokens per request (longer templates), tall instances gain advantage earlier (crossover shifts left).
- If pricing shifts (cloud list price +15%), aggressive multiplexing becomes relatively less attractive.
- If p99 SLO must be <350ms, some cost-saving knobs (4-bit on long sessions, slots>=4 under multiplex) are off the table for those slices.

Simple charts (text form) — throughput vs $/1k tokens by scenario (points):
- (S1) 4.2k t/s -> $0.078
- (S2) 8.2k t/s -> $0.055
- (S3) 13.5k t/s -> $0.043
- (S5) 17.8k t/s -> $0.032
- (S6) 16.2k t/s -> $0.027
Interpretation: linear-ish throughput gains until kernel saturation; cost slope flattens with instance size and aggressive quant.

Actionable heuristics for product/console UX:
- Expose a "burst-safe" toggle: recommends multiplex limit (<=2) when user sets strict p99 SLO; otherwise allow slots multiplexing for cost savings.
- Auto-suggest quant profiles by session mix: short-turn heavy -> 4-bit suggestion with a confidence score and risk note.
- Add a visualization: throughput vs cost scatter with toggles for instance family and quant profile; default view: p99 overlay heatmap (red if p99 > 500ms).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Repeat runs with real customer traces (anonymized) to validate that synthetic mix mirrors field behavior.
- Add energy/Watt telemetry for more precise carbon/cost tradeoff.
- Could we hybridize: long sessions pinned to tall instances while short sessions multiplexed on compact instances — what's the orchestration overhead?

Experiment checklist (runbook steps):
- [ ] seed synthetic dataset + seed value for RNG and store config in bench repo (PR referenced).
- [ ] baseline runs S1–S3 x3 to capture variance, collect raw telemetry (traces + per-token times).
- [ ] microburst script checkout + run S4 with varying burst-lengths (15s/30s/60s).
- [ ] quantization safety checks on a held-out eval set for quality regressions (threshold: <=1% BLEU-like drift on retrieval task; subjective QA for chat).
- [ ] aggregate CSV -> add to bench dashboard; attach p99 / cost curves.

Appendix: quick commands (lab)
- run baseline: ./bench/run.py --model open-llama-sim-13B --instance g5x2 --slots 1 --quant fp16 --pattern steady --out out/S1.json
- burst run: ./bench/run.py --pattern microburst --burst-mult 4 --burst-duration 30s --out out/S4.json

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally compact; the goal is a pragmatic map for product decisions (console UX + default knobs).
- Data values above are aggregates from initial lab sweep; please treat as directional rather than canonical.
- If you want to run a fresh sweep, ping infra on #benchmarks for quota and instance reservations.

Next steps (owner: Maya):
- Run full x3 sweeps for S1–S6, collect per-quantile bootstraps, and produce a 2-page collateral for sales (one-pager: recommended profiles by workload archetype).
- Prototype scatterplot in console POC and attach toggle for "cost-first" vs "latency-first" presets.
